problem:
A research container of mass $20\,\text{kg}$ falls vertically downward. Let $v(t)$ be the container's velocity, in meters per second, $t\ge 0$ seconds after the descent began, with downward taken as the positive direction.
The air resistance on the container is proportional to its velocity with a constant of proportionality $k>0$ and acts in the direction opposite to motion.
At a particular moment during the fall, the container’s velocity is $8\,\text{m/s}$ and instantaneous acceleration is $8.2\,{\text{m/s}}^{2}.$

Find the constant of proportionality $k,$ and the differential equation that best models the velocity. Assume the acceleration due to gravity is $g=9.8\,{\text{m/s}}^{2},$ and the only forces acting on the container are weight due to gravity and drag.

feedback.problem:
A supply pod of mass $30\,\text{kg}$ free-falls vertically downward. Let $v(t)$ be the pod's velocity, in meters per second, $t\ge 0$ seconds after the descent began, with downward taken as the positive direction.
The air resistance on the pod is proportional to its velocity with a constant of proportionality $k>0$ and acts in the direction opposite to motion.

Which differential equation best models the velocity? Assume that the acceleration due to gravity is $g,$ and the only forces acting on the pod are the weight due to gravity and drag.
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall Newton's second law, which states that the resultant force $F$ acting on a body equals the product of its mass $m$ and acceleration $a:$

$$
F=ma
$$

In our case, there are two forces acting on the pod:

- The force due to gravity, given by the weight $w$ of the pod, which equals

$$
\begin{aligned}w & =mg \\  & =30g\end{aligned}
$$

- The force due to drag (air resistance) $D,$ which is proportional to the velocity of the pod (and negative since it acts in the negative direction):

$$
D=-kv,
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality. Note that, since the drag, in $N=\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m/s}}^{2},$ is the product of the constant $k$ and velocity, in $\text{m/s},$ the units of $k$ are

$$
\frac{\text{N}}{\text{m/s}}=\frac{\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m/s}}^{2}}{\text{m/s}}=\text{kg/s}.
$$

Summing the forces, the resultant force acting on the pod is

$$
F=w+D=30g-kv.
$$

Also, recall that acceleration is the derivative of velocity: $a=\frac{dv}{dt}.$
Substituting this into Newton's second law, along with our expression for the resultant force on the pod, we have

$$
30g-kv=30\,\frac{dv}{dt}.
$$

Finally, simplifying and writing in standard form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}30\,\frac{dv}{dt}+kv & =30g \\ \frac{dv}{dt}+\frac{k}{30}v & =g.\end{aligned}
$$
